strengths: Rigorous theoretical contributions: Theorems 4.1-4.3 rigorously prove that existing guidance methods yield biased estimators that remain biased asymptotically, providing fundamental insights into a widely-used framework
Strong validation of consistency claim: Figure 3 convincingly shows CBG improves with increased compute while baselines plateau, directly validating the core theoretical claim

Principled solution framework with practical variants: Two estimators (gradient-based and gradient-free) provide flexibility; gradient-free variant elegantly handles non-differentiable objectives without computing model/likelihood gradients

Comprehensive experimental design: Bayesian Inference Benchmark substantially outperforms baselines (avg C2ST 0.527 vs. 0.803 for DPS) and comparisons include both diffusion-based and likelihood-free methods across 5 diverse tasks

Clear presentation and honest limitations discussion: Paper is well-written with effective visualizations; authors transparently acknowledge computational cost and discuss potential solutions (few-step diffusion models)
Sound mathematical proofs: Theorems use appropriate techniques (Taylor expansion with positive definite covariance, convolution theorem, Jensen's inequality) and are verified to be correct
weaknesses: Prohibitive computational cost severely limits practical adoption: Black hole imaging requires 2h40 per image on H100 GPU; requires K inner-loop samples at each of N timesteps (O(NM) cost). While pretraining few-step models is mentioned, it is not demonstrated

Marginal improvements on realistic tasks undermine value proposition: Black hole imaging shows only ~0.03 PSNR improvement over SOTA (26.10 vs. 26.07); no experiments on standard inverse problems with learned diffusion priors; improvement ratios do not justify 100× computational overhead

Gradient-based estimator practically infeasible: Table 1 shows substantial underperformance (0.681 vs. 0.527 avg C2ST); Section 5.3 analysis is limited to 1D toy case; high-dimensional behavior and self-normalization properties uncharacterized; authors explicitly avoid it for experiments

Insufficient evidence that calibration provides practical benefits: Even for scientific application (black hole imaging), realistic gains are negligible; no experiments on tasks where miscalibration demonstrably harms decisions; authors acknowledge natural images prioritize quality over calibration—a major application domain

Theoretical gaps in practical guidance: No convergence rate analysis; no finite-sample bounds on bias-variance tradeoff; unclear when K=1000 vs. K=100 is sufficient; Theorem 4.1 assumes Lipschitz prior and twice-differentiable likelihood (restrictive)

Limited experimental scope reduces generalizability: Bayesian Inference Benchmark uses only closed-form priors/likelihoods; no experiments on large-scale learned diffusion priors (e.g., ImageNet-scale models); black hole imaging uses only 100 test samples; hyperparameter selection (Table 4) shows high variance across tasks with vague justification

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: K ranges 100-10,000, M ranges 50-1000 across tasks with only 'trade-off between computational effort and image results' justification; sensitivity analysis missing; artificial N·K ≤ 10^5 budget restriction differs from practical tuning

Incremental estimator novelty: Reparameterization trick and REINFORCE are classical techniques; main contribution is application to diffused likelihood—important but somewhat incremental given strong theoretical contributions
